title: Energy, Momentum & Rotation
description: Work, energy conservation, power, impulse, collisions, torque, moments of inertia, rolling, angular momentum, gravitation, escape speed and SHM periods.

cards.title: A $50\,\mathrm{N}$ force pulls a sled $10\,\mathrm{m}$ across level ground, with the force directed $60^\circ$ above the horizontal. How much work does the force do, in joules?
cards.body:
$250\,\mathrm{J}$

$W = Fd\cos\theta = (50\,\mathrm{N})(10\,\mathrm{m})\cos 60^\circ$. Only the force component **along the displacement** does work.

Watch out: a force perpendicular to the motion, like the normal force here, does zero work.
cards.searchQuery: work done by force at an angle F d cos theta

cards.title: With the same constant braking force, by what factor does a car's stopping distance change if its initial speed doubles?
cards.body:
$4\times$ (it quadruples).

Work-energy theorem: $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$, so $fd = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ and $d \propto v^2$.

Why: doubling $v$ quadruples the kinetic energy that the braking force must remove.
cards.searchQuery: stopping distance scales with speed squared work energy

cards.title: An ideal spring with $k = 200\,\mathrm{N/m}$ is stretched $0.10\,\mathrm{m}$ from its relaxed length. How much elastic potential energy does it store, in joules?
cards.body:
$1.0\,\mathrm{J}$

$U = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(200\,\mathrm{N/m})(0.10\,\mathrm{m})^2$. Doubling the stretch quadruples the energy.

Watch out: using $kx$ gives the force ($20\,\mathrm{N}$), not the energy; and don't drop the $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
cards.searchQuery: elastic potential energy spring one half k x squared

cards.title: A block slides from rest down a frictionless ramp, dropping a vertical height $h$. What is its speed at the bottom?
cards.body:
$v = \sqrt{2gh}$, independent of the mass and of the ramp's shape.

Only gravity does work (the normal force is perpendicular to the motion), so mechanical energy is conserved: $mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$.

Watch out: with friction, some energy becomes thermal and $v$ is smaller.
cards.searchQuery: speed at bottom of frictionless ramp sqrt 2gh energy conservation

cards.title: A winch pulls a load at a constant $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ using a $500\,\mathrm{N}$ force along the direction of motion. What power does it deliver, in watts?
cards.body:
$1000\,\mathrm{W}$ ($1.0\,\mathrm{kW}$).

$P = \dfrac{dW}{dt} = Fv = (500\,\mathrm{N})(2.0\,\mathrm{m/s})$. If the force is at angle $\theta$ to the velocity, $P = Fv\cos\theta$.

Example: for scale, $1\,\mathrm{hp} \approx 746\,\mathrm{W}$.
cards.searchQuery: power equals force times velocity winch

cards.title: A $0.15\,\mathrm{kg}$ ball hits a wall at $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and rebounds straight back at $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is the magnitude of the impulse on the ball, in $\mathrm{N\cdot s}$?
cards.body:
$6.0\,\mathrm{N\cdot s}$ ($= 6.0\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m/s}$).

$J = \Delta p = m(v_f - v_i) = (0.15\,\mathrm{kg})\big(20 - (-20)\big)\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Watch out: the velocity reverses, so $\Delta v = 40\,\mathrm{m/s}$, not $0$.
Key idea: a bounce takes twice the impulse of just stopping.
cards.searchQuery: impulse ball bouncing off wall change in momentum

cards.title: A $3.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ cart moving at $4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ hits and sticks to a $1.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ cart at rest on a frictionless track. What is their speed afterward, in $\mathrm{m/s}$?
cards.body:
$3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$

Momentum is conserved (no net external horizontal force): $(3.0)(4.0) = (4.0)v$.

Why: kinetic energy is not conserved; it falls from $24\,\mathrm{J}$ to $18\,\mathrm{J}$. Sticking together (**perfectly inelastic**) loses the most kinetic energy that momentum conservation allows.
cards.searchQuery: perfectly inelastic collision carts stick together final speed

cards.title: In a head-on elastic collision, a moving ball strikes an identical ball at rest. What are their velocities just afterward?
cards.body:
The first ball **stops**; the second moves off with the first ball's original velocity.

Elastic means momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved, and for equal masses (one initially at rest) only this exchange satisfies both.

Watch out: in an inelastic collision only momentum is conserved.
cards.searchQuery: head on elastic collision equal masses velocities exchange

cards.title: A $20\,\mathrm{N}$ force is applied at the end of a $0.50\,\mathrm{m}$ wrench, at $30^\circ$ to the handle. What torque does it exert about the bolt, in $\mathrm{N\cdot m}$?
cards.body:
$5.0\,\mathrm{N\cdot m}$

$\tau = rF\sin\theta = (0.50\,\mathrm{m})(20\,\mathrm{N})\sin 30^\circ$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{r}$ (from the axis to the point of application) and $\vec{F}$.

Tip: pushing perpendicular to the handle maximizes $\tau$; pushing along it gives zero.
cards.searchQuery: torque r F sin theta wrench

cards.title: What is the moment of inertia of a thin uniform rod of mass $M$ and length $L$ about a perpendicular axis through one end?
cards.body:
$I = \tfrac{1}{3}ML^2$

Parallel-axis theorem: $I = I_{\text{cm}} + Md^2 = \tfrac{1}{12}ML^2 + M\left(\tfrac{L}{2}\right)^2 = \tfrac{1}{3}ML^2$.

Key idea: of all parallel axes, the one through the center of mass gives the smallest $I$.
cards.searchQuery: moment of inertia rod about end parallel axis theorem

cards.title: A hoop, a solid disk and a solid sphere roll without slipping from rest down the same incline. Which reaches the bottom first?
cards.body:
The **solid sphere**, then the disk, then the hoop.

Rolling without slipping ($v = \omega R$) gives $Mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}Mv^2\left(1 + \dfrac{I}{MR^2}\right)$, with $\dfrac{I}{MR^2} = \tfrac{2}{5}$ (sphere), $\tfrac{1}{2}$ (disk), $1$ (hoop).

Why: less energy tied up in rotation means faster translation. Mass and radius cancel.
cards.searchQuery: hoop disk sphere rolling down incline race which wins

cards.title: A spinning skater pulls her arms in, halving her moment of inertia. By what factor does her angular speed change? (Ignore friction.)
cards.body:
It **doubles**.

No external torque, so $L = I\omega$ is conserved: $I_1\omega_1 = \tfrac{1}{2}I_1\,\omega_2$ gives $\omega_2 = 2\omega_1$.

Why: her rotational kinetic energy, $\dfrac{L^2}{2I}$, also doubles; the extra energy comes from the work her muscles do pulling her arms in.
cards.searchQuery: skater pulls arms in angular momentum conservation spin faster

cards.title: Two masses attract gravitationally. If the distance between their centers triples, the force becomes what fraction of its original value?
cards.body:
$\tfrac{1}{9}$

Newton's law of gravitation: $F = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$, with $G = 6.67\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{N\cdot m^2/kg^2}$. Tripling $r$ divides $F$ by $3^2 = 9$.

Watch out: measure $r$ between the **centers**, not between the surfaces.
cards.searchQuery: Newton gravitation inverse square distance triples force

cards.title: What is the escape speed from the surface of a planet of mass $M$ and radius $R$? (Ignore air resistance.)
cards.body:
$v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$, about $11.2\,\mathrm{km/s}$ for Earth.

Set the total energy to zero: $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = 0$. It doesn't depend on the escaping object's mass or launch direction.

Key idea: it is $\sqrt{2}$ times the speed of a circular orbit at that radius.
cards.searchQuery: escape speed formula sqrt 2GM over R

cards.title: What is the period of an ideal mass–spring oscillator with mass $m$ and spring constant $k$?
cards.body:
$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$

It doesn't depend on the amplitude, or on $g$: hanging vertically gives the same period. The angular frequency is $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$.

Example: quadrupling the mass doubles the period.
cards.searchQuery: mass spring oscillator period 2 pi sqrt m over k

cards.title: What is the period of a simple pendulum of length $L$ swinging with small amplitude?
cards.body:
$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$

Valid for small angles ($\sin\theta \approx \theta$, roughly under $15^\circ$). It is independent of the bob's mass and, to this approximation, of the amplitude.

Example: quadrupling $L$ doubles $T$; on the Moon (smaller $g$) it swings more slowly.
cards.searchQuery: simple pendulum period formula small angle

cards.title: How is the work done by a constant force $\vec{F}$ on an object with displacement $\vec{d}$ defined?
cards.body:
$W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{d} = Fd\cos\theta$

Work is a **scalar**: only the component of force along the displacement counts, and $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{F}$ and $\vec{d}$.

Watch out: work can be positive, negative or zero; carrying a box at constant height does zero work on it (force and displacement are perpendicular).
cards.searchQuery: work done by constant force dot product definition

cards.title: Express one joule in SI base units.
cards.body:
$1\,\mathrm{J} = 1\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m^2/s^2}$

One joule is one newton-meter: $1\,\mathrm{J} = 1\,\mathrm{N\cdot m} = 1\,\mathrm{(kg\cdot m/s^2)\,m}$.

Tip: any energy expression must reduce to $\mathrm{kg\cdot m^2/s^2}$; this is a fast way to check a formula, such as $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$.
cards.searchQuery: joule unit SI base units kg m2 s2

cards.title: You lift a $3.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ box straight up $2.0\,\mathrm{m}$ at constant speed. How much work do you do on it, in joules to 3 significant figures? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$58.8\,\mathrm{J}$

Constant speed means your upward force equals the weight: $F = mg = 29.4\,\mathrm{N}$. Then $W = Fd = (29.4)(2.0)$.

Why: gravity does $-58.8\,\mathrm{J}$ on the box, so the net work is zero and its kinetic energy doesn't change.
cards.searchQuery: work done lifting box constant speed mgh

cards.title: Why does the net force on an object in uniform circular motion do zero work?
cards.body:
The force is **perpendicular** to the velocity (and displacement) at every instant.

$W = Fd\cos 90^\circ = 0$ for each small displacement, so the kinetic energy stays constant: only the direction of the velocity changes.

Watch out: if the speed changes, there is also a tangential force component, and that part does do work.
cards.searchQuery: centripetal force does no work perpendicular to velocity

cards.title: What is the sign of the work done by kinetic friction on a sliding block, and why?
cards.body:
**Negative**, because friction points opposite to the block's displacement.

$W = fd\cos 180^\circ = -fd$. The block's kinetic energy decreases by that amount.

Watch out: the work done by static friction on a rolling wheel's contact point is zero, and static friction can do positive work (it accelerates a crate on a truck bed).
cards.searchQuery: work done by kinetic friction negative sign

cards.title: State the work-energy theorem.
cards.body:
$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_f^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}mv_i^2$

The **net** work done by all forces on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.

Tip: it works for any forces, constant or not, and skips the details of the motion. Use it when the problem gives distances rather than times.
cards.searchQuery: work energy theorem net work equals change in kinetic energy

cards.title: What is the kinetic energy of an object of mass $m$ moving at speed $v$?
cards.body:
$K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$

Kinetic energy is a scalar and never negative; it does not depend on the direction of motion.

Why: $\int F\,dx = \int mv\,dv = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ for an object accelerated from rest.
cards.searchQuery: kinetic energy formula one half m v squared

cards.title: A $1200\,\mathrm{kg}$ car moves at $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is its kinetic energy, in joules?
cards.body:
$2.4\times10^5\,\mathrm{J}$

$K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(1200)(20)^2 = 240\,000\,\mathrm{J}$.

Watch out: square only the speed, not the product $mv$.
cards.searchQuery: kinetic energy of a car numeric one half m v squared

cards.title: If an object's speed doubles, by what factors do its kinetic energy and its momentum change?
cards.body:
Kinetic energy $\times 4$; momentum $\times 2$.

$K \propto v^2$ but $p = mv \propto v$.

Watch out: this is why the stopping distance (set by energy) grows faster than the stopping time (set by momentum) at higher speed.
cards.searchQuery: doubling speed kinetic energy quadruples momentum doubles

cards.title: A $2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ cart starts from rest and a net force does $25\,\mathrm{J}$ of work on it. What is its final speed, in $\mathrm{m/s}$?
cards.body:
$5.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$

Work-energy theorem: $W_{\text{net}} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, so $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2W}{m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(25)}{2.0}}$.

Tip: you don't need to know the force or the distance, only the net work.
cards.searchQuery: speed from net work done on cart starting from rest

cards.title: On a graph of force along the displacement versus position, what does the area under the curve represent?
cards.body:
The **work** done by the force.

$W = \int F\,dx$. Area above the axis is positive work; area below is negative.

Example: for a spring, the triangle under $F = kx$ from $0$ to $x$ has area $\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$.
cards.searchQuery: area under force versus position graph is work

cards.title: What is Hooke's law for the force an ideal spring exerts when stretched or compressed by $x$ from its relaxed length?
cards.body:
$F = -kx$

The force is **restoring**: it always points back toward the relaxed length. The spring constant $k$ has units $\mathrm{N/m}$.

Watch out: the minus sign gives direction; the magnitude is $kx$. Real springs obey the law only for small deformations.
cards.searchQuery: Hooke law spring force F equals minus kx restoring

cards.title: A spring with $k = 100\,\mathrm{N/m}$ is stretched from $0.10\,\mathrm{m}$ to $0.30\,\mathrm{m}$ beyond its relaxed length. How much work does an external force do, in joules?
cards.body:
$4.0\,\mathrm{J}$

$W = \tfrac{1}{2}k(x_2^2 - x_1^2) = \tfrac{1}{2}(100)(0.30^2 - 0.10^2) = 50(0.08)$.

Watch out: don't use $\tfrac{1}{2}k(x_2 - x_1)^2$; the energy depends on the squares of the positions, not of the change.
cards.searchQuery: work to stretch spring between two positions one half k difference of squares

cards.title: A $0.50\,\mathrm{kg}$ block is released by a spring ($k = 400\,\mathrm{N/m}$) compressed $0.10\,\mathrm{m}$; no friction. Its speed leaving the spring, in $\mathrm{m/s}$ to 3 s.f.?
cards.body:
$2.83\,\mathrm{m/s}$

All the stored energy becomes kinetic: $\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, so $v = x\sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}} = 0.10\sqrt{800}$.

Check: the stored energy is $\tfrac{1}{2}(400)(0.10)^2 = 2.0\,\mathrm{J}$, and $\tfrac{1}{2}(0.50)(2.83)^2 = 2.0\,\mathrm{J}$.
cards.searchQuery: spring launches block speed energy conservation compressed spring

cards.title: A $10\,\mathrm{kg}$ crate slides $5.0\,\mathrm{m}$ across a level floor with $\mu_k = 0.30$. What work does friction do on it, in joules? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$-147\,\mathrm{J}$

$f = \mu_k mg = (0.30)(10)(9.8) = 29.4\,\mathrm{N}$, and friction opposes the motion: $W = -fd = -(29.4)(5.0)$.

Why: the crate's kinetic energy falls by $147\,\mathrm{J}$; that amount is transferred to thermal energy of the crate and floor.
cards.searchQuery: work done by friction on sliding crate negative numeric

cards.title: What is the gravitational potential energy of a mass $m$ at height $h$ above a chosen reference level, near Earth's surface?
cards.body:
$U = mgh$

Only changes in $U$ matter, so the reference level ($h = 0$) is arbitrary. It is valid when $g$ is nearly constant over the height.

Watch out: for large distances from Earth use $U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$ instead.
cards.searchQuery: gravitational potential energy mgh reference level

cards.title: What is the gravitational potential energy of a $2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ object $5.0\,\mathrm{m}$ above the floor (taking the floor as zero), in joules? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$98\,\mathrm{J}$

$U = mgh = (2.0)(9.8)(5.0)$.

Tip: if you pick a different reference level, $U$ changes, but the difference $\Delta U$ between two points does not.
cards.searchQuery: gravitational potential energy numeric 2 kg 5 m

cards.title: What makes a force **conservative**?
cards.body:
The work it does between two points is **independent of the path**, equivalently zero around any closed loop.

Only conservative forces have a potential energy function $U$, with $W = -\Delta U$.

Example: gravity and ideal springs are conservative.
Watch out: friction and air drag are not; the work they do depends on the path length.
cards.searchQuery: conservative force definition path independent work

cards.title: A particle has potential energy $U(x) = 3.0x^2$ (joules, with $x$ in meters). What is the force on it at $x = 2.0\,\mathrm{m}$, in newtons?
cards.body:
$-12\,\mathrm{N}$ (toward $-x$).

$F_x = -\dfrac{dU}{dx} = -6.0x$, so $F_x(2.0) = -12\,\mathrm{N}$.

Key idea: force points toward lower potential energy; the slope of $U$ gives the force's magnitude.
cards.searchQuery: force from potential energy negative derivative dU dx

cards.title: Under what condition is the total mechanical energy $K + U$ of a system conserved?
cards.body:
When only **conservative forces** do work.

Then $K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$. If nonconservative forces act, $K_i + U_i + W_{\text{nc}} = K_f + U_f$.

Watch out: forces that do no work (such as the normal force on a ramp) don't spoil conservation.
cards.searchQuery: conservation of mechanical energy condition conservative forces

cards.title: A pendulum bob on a $1.0\,\mathrm{m}$ string is released from rest at $60^\circ$ from vertical. Its speed at the bottom, in $\mathrm{m/s}$ to 3 significant figures? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$3.13\,\mathrm{m/s}$

The bob drops $h = L(1 - \cos 60^\circ) = 0.50\,\mathrm{m}$, so $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2(9.8)(0.50)}$.

Watch out: $h$ is the vertical drop, not the arc length. The tension does no work, since it is always perpendicular to the motion.
cards.searchQuery: pendulum bottom speed released at 60 degrees energy conservation

cards.title: Three identical balls are thrown from the same height at the same speed, one up, one down and one horizontally. How do their speeds just before hitting the ground compare? (No air resistance.)
cards.body:
All the **same**: $v = \sqrt{v_0^2 + 2gh}$.

Energy conservation only needs the initial speed and the vertical drop: $\tfrac{1}{2}mv_0^2 + mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$. The direction of launch doesn't appear.

Watch out: their landing times and angles still differ; only the speeds match.
cards.searchQuery: balls thrown different directions same height same impact speed energy

cards.title: A frictionless coaster car starts from rest at $30\,\mathrm{m}$ height. Its speed at $10\,\mathrm{m}$ height, in $\mathrm{m/s}$ to 3 significant figures? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$19.8\,\mathrm{m/s}$

The car has dropped $20\,\mathrm{m}$, so $v = \sqrt{2g\,\Delta h} = \sqrt{2(9.8)(20)} = \sqrt{392}$.

Tip: only the height difference matters, not the track's shape or the car's mass.
cards.searchQuery: roller coaster speed at height energy conservation

cards.title: A frictionless block slides from rest into a vertical loop of radius $R$. What minimum release height above the loop's bottom, in units of $R$, keeps it on the track at the top?
cards.body:
$2.5R$

At the top the minimum speed satisfies $mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{R}$, so $v^2 = gR$. Energy conservation from release to the top (height $2R$): $mgh = mg(2R) + \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, so $h = 2R + \dfrac{R}{2}$.

Watch out: this is for a sliding block; a rolling ball needs a greater height, because some energy goes into rotation.
cards.searchQuery: vertical loop minimum release height 2.5 R

cards.title: A $2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ block slides from rest down a rough ramp, dropping $1.5\,\mathrm{m}$, and arrives at $4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Thermal energy produced, in J? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$13.4\,\mathrm{J}$

Initial energy: $mgh = (2.0)(9.8)(1.5) = 29.4\,\mathrm{J}$. Final kinetic energy: $\tfrac{1}{2}(2.0)(4.0)^2 = 16\,\mathrm{J}$.

Why: the difference, $29.4 - 16 = 13.4\,\mathrm{J}$, is the magnitude of the work done by friction.
cards.searchQuery: energy lost to friction block sliding down ramp thermal energy

cards.title: A $0.50\,\mathrm{kg}$ mass hangs at rest from a vertical spring with $k = 49\,\mathrm{N/m}$. How far does the spring stretch, in meters? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$0.10\,\mathrm{m}$

At equilibrium the spring force balances the weight: $kx = mg$, so $x = \dfrac{(0.50)(9.8)}{49}$.

Tip: for vertical oscillations, measure displacement from this equilibrium point and gravity drops out of the motion.
cards.searchQuery: hanging mass spring equilibrium stretch kx equals mg

cards.title: A $0.50\,\mathrm{kg}$ mass is released from rest on a vertical spring ($k = 49\,\mathrm{N/m}$) at its relaxed length. What is the maximum stretch, in meters? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$0.20\,\mathrm{m}$

At the lowest point the speed is zero: $mgx = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$, so $x = \dfrac{2mg}{k} = \dfrac{2(4.9)}{49}$.

Key idea: that is twice the equilibrium stretch of $0.10\,\mathrm{m}$; the mass oscillates symmetrically about equilibrium.
cards.searchQuery: mass released from relaxed vertical spring maximum stretch 2mg over k

cards.title: On a plot of potential energy $U(x)$, what kind of equilibrium does a local minimum represent?
cards.body:
**Stable** equilibrium.

At a point where $\dfrac{dU}{dx} = 0$ the force is zero. At a minimum, a small displacement produces a restoring force back toward it.

Watch out: at a local maximum the equilibrium is unstable, because any displacement is pushed further away.
cards.searchQuery: potential energy curve local minimum stable equilibrium

cards.title: On an energy diagram, what is true of a particle's kinetic energy at a classical turning point?
cards.body:
It is **zero**: the total energy equals the potential energy there.

$E = K + U$ and $K \ge 0$, so the particle can only be where $U(x) \le E$. At the boundary, $K = 0$ and the particle momentarily stops before reversing.

Example: a pendulum bob at the top of its swing.
cards.searchQuery: turning point energy diagram kinetic energy zero total energy equals potential

cards.title: How many joules are in one kilowatt-hour?
cards.body:
$3.6\times10^6\,\mathrm{J}$

$1\,\mathrm{kWh} = (1000\,\mathrm{W})(3600\,\mathrm{s})$.

Watch out: the kilowatt-hour is a unit of **energy**, not power.
cards.searchQuery: kilowatt hour in joules 3.6 million

cards.title: How is average power related to work and time?
cards.body:
$P = \dfrac{W}{\Delta t}$

The SI unit is the watt: $1\,\mathrm{W} = 1\,\mathrm{J/s}$. Instantaneous power is $P = \dfrac{dW}{dt}$.

Tip: power is the *rate* of energy transfer. Doing the same work faster takes more power.
cards.searchQuery: average power work divided by time watt

cards.title: A $70\,\mathrm{kg}$ person climbs $3.0\,\mathrm{m}$ of stairs in $5.0\,\mathrm{s}$. What average power does she use against gravity, in watts to 3 significant figures? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$412\,\mathrm{W}$

$P = \dfrac{mgh}{t} = \dfrac{(70)(9.8)(3.0)}{5.0} = \dfrac{2058}{5.0}\,\mathrm{W}$.

Watch out: this counts only the work against gravity; her muscles actually use more power, because the body is far from 100% efficient.
cards.searchQuery: power climbing stairs mgh over time numeric

cards.title: Express one watt in SI base units.
cards.body:
$1\,\mathrm{W} = 1\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m^2/s^3}$

Start from $1\,\mathrm{W} = 1\,\mathrm{J/s}$ and $1\,\mathrm{J} = 1\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m^2/s^2}$.

Tip: power is force times velocity, $\mathrm{N\cdot m/s}$, which gives the same base units.
cards.searchQuery: watt in SI base units kg m2 s3

cards.title: A car's engine delivers $20\,\mathrm{kW}$ to the road while it moves at a constant $25\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is the forward force on the car, in newtons?
cards.body:
$800\,\mathrm{N}$

$P = Fv$, so $F = \dfrac{P}{v} = \dfrac{20\,000\,\mathrm{W}}{25\,\mathrm{m/s}}$.

Key idea: at constant speed this forward force equals the total resistive force (drag plus rolling friction).
cards.searchQuery: force from power and velocity car constant speed P equals Fv

cards.title: A vehicle at constant speed overcomes air drag $D \propto v^2$. By what factor does the power needed against drag grow if the speed doubles?
cards.body:
$8\times$

$P = Dv \propto v^2\cdot v = v^3$, so doubling the speed multiplies the power by $2^3 = 8$.

Why: this is why fuel use climbs steeply at highway speeds.
cards.searchQuery: power against air drag proportional to speed cubed

cards.title: What is the momentum of an object of mass $m$ moving with velocity $\vec{v}$, and what are its SI units?
cards.body:
$\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$, in $\mathrm{kg\cdot m/s}$.

Momentum is a **vector** that points along the velocity. The units $\mathrm{kg\cdot m/s}$ are the same as $\mathrm{N\cdot s}$.

Watch out: unlike kinetic energy, momentum has a direction and can cancel between objects.
cards.searchQuery: momentum definition p equals mv units

cards.title: A $0.145\,\mathrm{kg}$ baseball moves at $40\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is its momentum, in $\mathrm{kg\cdot m/s}$?
cards.body:
$5.8\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m/s}$

$p = mv = (0.145)(40)$.

Tip: $\mathrm{kg\cdot m/s}$ is the same unit as $\mathrm{N\cdot s}$, so this is also the impulse needed to stop the ball.
cards.searchQuery: momentum of baseball numeric mass times velocity

cards.title: State the impulse-momentum theorem.
cards.body:
$\vec{J} = \int \vec{F}\,dt = \Delta\vec{p}$

The impulse of the net force equals the change in momentum. For a constant force, $\vec{J} = \vec{F}\,\Delta t$.

Tip: use it when a problem gives force and time (or contact time) instead of distance.
cards.searchQuery: impulse momentum theorem integral of force equals change in momentum

cards.title: On a graph of force versus time, what does the area under the curve represent?
cards.body:
The **impulse**, which equals the change in momentum.

$J = \int F\,dt$. Area below the axis counts as negative.

Example: a rectangular pulse of $10\,\mathrm{N}$ lasting $2.0\,\mathrm{s}$ delivers $20\,\mathrm{N\cdot s}$.
cards.searchQuery: area under force versus time graph impulse

cards.title: A $0.50\,\mathrm{kg}$ ball at rest is kicked and leaves at $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ after $0.010\,\mathrm{s}$ of contact. What is the average force, in newtons?
cards.body:
$1000\,\mathrm{N}$

$F_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{(0.50)(20)}{0.010}$.

Watch out: the peak force during the kick is larger than this average.
cards.searchQuery: average force from impulse kicked ball contact time

cards.title: Why does an airbag reduce injury in a crash, in terms of impulse?
cards.body:
It **lengthens the stopping time**, so the average force is smaller for the same $\Delta p$.

$F_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$: with the same change in momentum, a longer $\Delta t$ means a smaller force.

Example: catching a fast ball by letting your hand move back with it works the same way.
cards.searchQuery: airbag longer stopping time reduces force impulse

cards.title: How is Newton's second law written in terms of momentum?
cards.body:
$\sum\vec{F} = \dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$

The net force equals the rate of change of momentum. For constant mass it reduces to $\sum\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$.

Tip: this form also handles systems whose mass changes, such as rockets.
cards.searchQuery: Newton second law momentum form F equals dp dt

cards.title: When is the total momentum of a system conserved?
cards.body:
When the net **external** force on the system is zero.

Internal forces come in third-law pairs and cancel in the total, so they can't change it.

Watch out: momentum can be conserved in one direction only, for example horizontally when the only external force (gravity) is vertical.
cards.searchQuery: conservation of momentum condition net external force zero

cards.title: A free, initially stationary $4.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ gun fires a $0.010\,\mathrm{kg}$ bullet at $400\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is the gun's recoil speed, in $\mathrm{m/s}$?
cards.body:
$1.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, opposite to the bullet.

Total momentum starts at zero and stays zero: $0 = (0.010)(400) + (4.0)v$, so $|v| = \dfrac{4.0}{4.0}$.

Why: the bullet carries most of the kinetic energy; the gun has the same momentum magnitude but much lower speed.
cards.searchQuery: gun recoil speed conservation of momentum bullet

cards.title: Express an object's kinetic energy in terms of its momentum $p$ and mass $m$.
cards.body:
$K = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$

Substitute $v = p/m$ into $K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$.

Tip: for equal momenta, the lighter object has more kinetic energy.
cards.searchQuery: kinetic energy in terms of momentum p squared over 2m

cards.title: A rocket expels exhaust at $3000\,\mathrm{m/s}$ relative to itself, at a rate of $2.0\,\mathrm{kg/s}$. What thrust does this produce, in newtons?
cards.body:
$6000\,\mathrm{N}$

Thrust $= v_{\text{ex}}\left|\dfrac{dm}{dt}\right| = (3000)(2.0)$.

Why: each second, $2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ of gas gains $3000\,\mathrm{m/s}$ of momentum, and the rocket gains an equal and opposite amount.
cards.searchQuery: rocket thrust exhaust speed mass flow rate

cards.title: Skaters of $60\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $40\,\mathrm{kg}$ push apart from rest on frictionless ice. The $60\,\mathrm{kg}$ skater moves at $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. How fast is the other, in $\mathrm{m/s}$?
cards.body:
$3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, in the opposite direction.

Total momentum stays zero: $(60)(2.0) = (40)v$.

Key idea: the lighter skater ends up faster, in inverse proportion to mass.
cards.searchQuery: two skaters push apart conservation of momentum speeds

cards.title: A $2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ mass sits at $x = 0$ and a $4.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ mass sits at $x = 6.0\,\mathrm{m}$. Where is the center of mass, in meters?
cards.body:
$x_{\text{cm}} = 4.0\,\mathrm{m}$

$x_{\text{cm}} = \dfrac{\sum m_ix_i}{\sum m_i} = \dfrac{(2.0)(0) + (4.0)(6.0)}{6.0}$.

Tip: the center of mass is always closer to the heavier object.
cards.searchQuery: center of mass two particles weighted average position

cards.title: A projectile explodes in mid-air. What path does the center of mass of the fragments follow (before any hits the ground)?
cards.body:
The **same parabola** the unexploded projectile would have followed.

The explosion's forces are internal, so only gravity affects the system's total momentum, hence its center-of-mass motion.

Watch out: individual fragments follow different paths, and the first one to land does not change the center of mass's path until it hits.
cards.searchQuery: center of mass of exploding projectile follows same parabola

cards.title: For a system of particles, how does the net external force relate to the center-of-mass motion?
cards.body:
$\sum\vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = M\vec{a}_{\text{cm}}$

Here $M$ is the total mass. The center of mass accelerates as though all the mass were concentrated there and all external forces acted on it.

Key idea: internal forces never change the motion of the center of mass.
cards.searchQuery: net external force equals total mass times center of mass acceleration

cards.title: What distinguishes an elastic collision from an inelastic one?
cards.body:
In an **elastic** collision kinetic energy is conserved; in an **inelastic** one it is not.

Momentum is conserved in both (when no net external force acts).

Watch out: "inelastic" does not mean the objects stick; sticking together (perfectly inelastic) is just the case of maximum kinetic energy loss.
cards.searchQuery: elastic versus inelastic collision kinetic energy conserved

cards.title: Masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ with velocities $v_1$ and $v_2$ collide in 1D and stick together. What is their common velocity afterward?
cards.body:
$v_f = \dfrac{m_1v_1 + m_2v_2}{m_1 + m_2}$

Momentum conservation with a single final velocity. Velocities are signed.

Watch out: a mass moving the opposite way enters with a negative $v$.
cards.searchQuery: perfectly inelastic collision final velocity formula momentum

cards.title: A $2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ puck moving at $6.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ hits and sticks to an identical puck at rest. How much kinetic energy is lost, in joules?
cards.body:
$18\,\mathrm{J}$

Momentum: $(2.0)(6.0) = (4.0)v$, so $v = 3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Kinetic energy: $\tfrac{1}{2}(2.0)(6.0)^2 = 36\,\mathrm{J}$ before and $\tfrac{1}{2}(4.0)(3.0)^2 = 18\,\mathrm{J}$ after.

Why: the lost $18\,\mathrm{J}$ becomes thermal energy and deformation.
cards.searchQuery: kinetic energy lost perfectly inelastic collision pucks numeric

cards.title: An object hits an identical object at rest and they stick together. What fraction of the initial kinetic energy is lost?
cards.body:
One half, $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

The final speed is $v/2$, so the final kinetic energy is $\tfrac{1}{2}(2m)(v/2)^2 = \tfrac{1}{4}mv^2$, half of the initial $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$.

Tip: this is a handy check: the answer doesn't depend on the masses' values, only on their equality.
cards.searchQuery: fraction of kinetic energy lost equal masses stick together

cards.title: In a 1D elastic collision, how does the relative speed of the objects after the collision compare with before?
cards.body:
The relative speed is **the same**, with the direction reversed.

Combining momentum and energy conservation gives $v_{1i} - v_{2i} = -(v_{1f} - v_{2f})$.

Tip: this linear relation plus momentum conservation is often easier than solving the quadratic energy equation.
cards.searchQuery: elastic collision relative speed of approach equals separation

cards.title: A light ball hits a much heavier stationary ball head-on in an elastic collision. What happens to the light ball?
cards.body:
It **bounces back** with nearly its original speed; the heavy ball barely moves.

For $m_1 \ll m_2$: $v_{1f} = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}v_{1i} \approx -v_{1i}$.

Example: a ball bouncing off a wall (like the Earth).
cards.searchQuery: light object hits heavy stationary object elastic collision bounces back

cards.title: A heavy object hits a much lighter stationary object head-on in an elastic collision. What is the light object's final speed, approximately?
cards.body:
About **twice** the heavy object's speed.

For $m_1 \gg m_2$: $v_{2f} = \dfrac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2}v_{1i} \approx 2v_{1i}$, while the heavy object barely slows.

Example: a bowling ball hitting a table-tennis ball flings it off at about twice the bowling ball's speed.
cards.searchQuery: heavy object hits light stationary object elastic collision twice speed

cards.title: A $2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ block at $3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ hits a $1.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ block at rest, head-on and elastically. The $1.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ block's speed afterward, in $\mathrm{m/s}$?
cards.body:
$4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$

$v_{2f} = \dfrac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2}v_{1i} = \dfrac{2(2.0)}{3.0}(3.0)$. The $2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ block continues at $v_{1f} = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}v_{1i} = 1.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Check: momentum is $6.0$ before and $(2.0)(1.0) + (1.0)(4.0) = 6.0$ after.
cards.searchQuery: 1D elastic collision numeric 2 kg and 1 kg final velocity

cards.title: A ball dropped from $1.0\,\mathrm{m}$ onto the floor bounces back up to $0.64\,\mathrm{m}$. What is the coefficient of restitution $e$?
cards.body:
$e = 0.80$

$e = \dfrac{\text{speed after}}{\text{speed before}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{h'}{h}} = \sqrt{0.64}$.

Why: speed is proportional to the square root of height. $e = 1$ is perfectly elastic; $e = 0$ is perfectly inelastic.
cards.searchQuery: coefficient of restitution bounce height square root ratio

cards.title: A bullet embeds in a hanging block (ballistic pendulum). Which quantity is conserved during the embedding: momentum, kinetic energy, or both?
cards.body:
Only **momentum**.

The embedding is perfectly inelastic and very brief, so momentum is conserved (external forces are negligible during it) but kinetic energy is not.

Tip: afterward, the swing up is a separate stage where mechanical energy of block and bullet is conserved.
cards.searchQuery: ballistic pendulum which quantity conserved momentum kinetic energy

cards.title: A $0.010\,\mathrm{kg}$ bullet at $400\,\mathrm{m/s}$ embeds in a hanging $0.990\,\mathrm{kg}$ block. How high does the block rise, in meters to 2 significant figures? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$0.82\,\mathrm{m}$

Stage 1 (momentum): $(0.010)(400) = (1.000)v$, so $v = 4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Stage 2 (energy): $h = \dfrac{v^2}{2g} = \dfrac{16}{19.6}$.

Watch out: don't apply energy conservation to the whole process; energy is lost in stage 1.
cards.searchQuery: ballistic pendulum height numeric bullet block

cards.title: How do you apply momentum conservation to a two-dimensional collision?
cards.body:
Conserve momentum **separately** along each axis.

$\sum p_x$ and $\sum p_y$ are each unchanged, giving two equations.

Tip: choose axes so one component is simple; for example, make $x$ the incoming direction.
cards.searchQuery: two dimensional collision momentum conserved in each component

cards.title: A moving ball hits an identical stationary ball off-center in an elastic collision. What is the angle between their velocities afterward?
cards.body:
$90^\circ$

Momentum gives $\vec{v}_0 = \vec{v}_1 + \vec{v}_2$ and energy gives $v_0^2 = v_1^2 + v_2^2$. Together they say the velocities are perpendicular (Pythagoras).

Watch out: this holds only for equal masses and a stationary target; head-on is the special case where one ball stops.
cards.searchQuery: equal mass elastic collision 2D right angle after collision

cards.title: In a car-truck collision, how do the impulses on the two vehicles compare, and who has the larger change in velocity?
cards.body:
The impulses are **equal and opposite**; the lighter car has the larger $\Delta v$.

Third law: the contact forces are equal and opposite for the same time interval, so $\Delta p_1 = -\Delta p_2$.

Why: with $\Delta p = m\,\Delta v$ the same, the smaller mass undergoes the larger velocity change.
cards.searchQuery: collision equal and opposite impulses lighter vehicle larger velocity change

cards.title: Besides $\tau = rF\sin\theta$, how can the magnitude of a torque be written using the lever arm?
cards.body:
$\tau = r_\perp F$

The lever arm $r_\perp$ is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action of the force; $r_\perp = r\sin\theta$.

Tip: a force whose line of action passes through the axis has zero lever arm and exerts no torque.
cards.searchQuery: torque lever arm perpendicular distance definition

cards.title: A net torque of $6.0\,\mathrm{N\cdot m}$ acts on a wheel with moment of inertia $2.0\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m^2}$. What is its angular acceleration, in $\mathrm{rad/s^2}$?
cards.body:
$3.0\,\mathrm{rad/s^2}$

Rotational second law: $\sum\tau = I\alpha$, so $\alpha = \dfrac{6.0}{2.0}$.

Key idea: it is the rotational analogue of $F = ma$, with torque, moment of inertia and angular acceleration in place of force, mass and acceleration.
cards.searchQuery: net torque angular acceleration moment of inertia tau equals I alpha

cards.title: Two $1.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ masses are attached to a very light rod, each $0.50\,\mathrm{m}$ from the rotation axis. What is the system's moment of inertia, in $\mathrm{kg\cdot m^2}$?
cards.body:
$0.50\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m^2}$

$I = \sum m_ir_i^2 = (1.0)(0.50)^2 + (1.0)(0.50)^2$.

Watch out: distances are squared, so moving mass outward raises $I$ quickly.
cards.searchQuery: moment of inertia two point masses sum m r squared

cards.title: What is the moment of inertia of a uniform solid disk (or cylinder) of mass $M$ and radius $R$ about its central axis?
cards.body:
$I = \tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$

A hoop of the same mass and radius has the larger $I = MR^2$, because all its mass sits at the full radius.

Tip: a smaller $I/MR^2$ means less rotational energy for the same speed, so a disk rolls down a ramp faster than a hoop.
cards.searchQuery: moment of inertia solid disk one half M R squared

cards.title: A flywheel with $I = 0.50\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m^2}$ spins at $4.0\,\mathrm{rad/s}$. What is its rotational kinetic energy, in joules?
cards.body:
$4.0\,\mathrm{J}$

$K = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.50)(4.0)^2$.

Watch out: $\omega$ must be in rad/s, not revolutions per minute.
cards.searchQuery: rotational kinetic energy one half I omega squared numeric

cards.title: A solid sphere rolls without slipping. What fraction of its total kinetic energy is rotational?
cards.body:
$\tfrac{2}{7}$

Rotational: $\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\tfrac{2}{5}MR^2\cdot\dfrac{v^2}{R^2} = \tfrac{1}{5}Mv^2$. Translational: $\tfrac{1}{2}Mv^2$.

Why: the fraction is $\dfrac{1/5}{1/2 + 1/5} = \dfrac{2}{7}$. For a hoop it is $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
cards.searchQuery: solid sphere rolling fraction of kinetic energy rotational 2/7

cards.title: A solid sphere rolls without slipping down a $30^\circ$ incline. What is the acceleration of its center, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$3.5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$

For rolling without slipping, $a = \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1 + I/MR^2} = \dfrac{(9.8)(0.50)}{1 + 2/5}$.

Watch out: it is less than the frictionless sliding value $g\sin\theta = 4.9\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, because some energy goes into rotation.
cards.searchQuery: solid sphere rolling down incline acceleration 5/7 g sin theta

cards.title: A turntable ($I = 2.0\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m^2}$) spins at $6.0\,\mathrm{rad/s}$. Clay dropped on it adds $1.0\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m^2}$ to $I$. What is the new angular speed, in $\mathrm{rad/s}$?
cards.body:
$4.0\,\mathrm{rad/s}$

No external torque, so $L = I\omega$ is conserved: $(2.0)(6.0) = (3.0)\omega$.

Watch out: kinetic energy is not conserved; this is a rotational perfectly inelastic collision, and energy is lost.
cards.searchQuery: turntable angular momentum conservation added moment of inertia

cards.title: A $40\,\mathrm{kg}$ child sits $2.0\,\mathrm{m}$ from the pivot of a balanced seesaw. How far from the pivot, in meters, must a $50\,\mathrm{kg}$ child sit on the other side?
cards.body:
$1.6\,\mathrm{m}$

Rotational equilibrium requires equal torques about the pivot: $(40)g(2.0) = (50)g\,d$, so $d = \dfrac{80}{50}$.

Tip: $g$ cancels, so the answer is the same on any planet.
cards.searchQuery: seesaw balance torque equilibrium distance from pivot

cards.title: At a height above Earth's surface equal to Earth's radius, what is the free-fall acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$? (Surface value $g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.)
cards.body:
$2.45\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$

The distance from Earth's center is $2R$, and $g \propto 1/r^2$, so $g' = \dfrac{9.8}{2^2}$.

Watch out: the distance is measured from the center, not from the surface.
cards.searchQuery: gravitational acceleration at altitude equal to earth radius inverse square

cards.title: What is the speed of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius $r$ about a mass $M$?
cards.body:
$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$

Gravity supplies the centripetal force: $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2} = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. The satellite's mass cancels.

Example: just above Earth's surface (ignoring air) this is about $7.9\,\mathrm{km/s}$.
cards.searchQuery: circular orbital speed sqrt GM over r

cards.title: Planet B orbits a star at four times the orbital radius of planet A. By what factor is B's orbital period longer?
cards.body:
$8$

Kepler's third law: $T^2 \propto r^3$, so $T \propto r^{3/2}$ and $T_B/T_A = 4^{3/2}$.

Tip: $4^{3/2} = (\sqrt{4})^3 = 8$.
cards.searchQuery: Kepler third law period scales with radius to the 3/2

cards.title: What is the gravitational potential energy of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ a distance $r$ apart, with $U = 0$ at infinite separation?
cards.body:
$U = -\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r}$

It is **negative** because the masses are bound: work must be done on them to separate them to infinity.

Watch out: $U = mgh$ is only the small-height approximation of the change in this expression.
cards.searchQuery: gravitational potential energy negative GMm over r

cards.title: Why do astronauts in the International Space Station float, even though gravity there is about 90% of its surface value?
cards.body:
They and the station are in **continuous free fall**.

They fall toward Earth but also move sideways fast enough that the ground curves away beneath them.

Watch out: the apparent weightlessness comes from the lack of a normal force, not from the absence of gravity.
cards.searchQuery: astronauts weightless in orbit free fall not zero gravity

cards.title: What condition on the net force defines simple harmonic motion?
cards.body:
A **restoring force proportional to displacement**: $F = -kx$.

This gives $a = -\omega^2x$ with $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$, and sinusoidal motion $x = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)$.

Watch out: a constant restoring force, or one that grows as $x^2$, would not give SHM.
cards.searchQuery: simple harmonic motion defining condition restoring force proportional to displacement

cards.title: A $0.50\,\mathrm{kg}$ mass on an ideal spring with $k = 50\,\mathrm{N/m}$ oscillates. What is its period, in seconds to 3 significant figures?
cards.body:
$0.628\,\mathrm{s}$

$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{0.50}{50}} = 2\pi(0.10)$.

Tip: $\omega = \sqrt{k/m} = 10\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, so $T = 2\pi/\omega$.
cards.searchQuery: mass spring period numeric 0.5 kg 50 N/m

cards.title: An oscillator has amplitude $A = 0.10\,\mathrm{m}$ and angular frequency $\omega = 5.0\,\mathrm{rad/s}$. What is its maximum speed, in $\mathrm{m/s}$?
cards.body:
$0.50\,\mathrm{m/s}$

$v_{\max} = A\omega = (0.10)(5.0)$, reached as it passes through equilibrium.

Example: the maximum acceleration is $A\omega^2 = 2.5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, at the turning points.
cards.searchQuery: SHM maximum speed amplitude times angular frequency

cards.title: A mass-spring oscillator is at $x = A/2$. What fraction of its total energy is kinetic?
cards.body:
$\tfrac{3}{4}$

Total energy is $\tfrac{1}{2}kA^2$; the potential energy at $x = A/2$ is $\tfrac{1}{2}k(A/2)^2 = \tfrac{1}{4}$ of that.

Why: the remaining $\tfrac{3}{4}$ is kinetic, since $K + U$ is constant.
cards.searchQuery: SHM kinetic energy fraction at half amplitude three quarters

cards.title: What is the period of a simple pendulum of length $1.0\,\mathrm{m}$ with small swings, in seconds to 3 significant figures? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
cards.body:
$2.01\,\mathrm{s}$

$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{1.0}{9.8}}$.

Tip: a pendulum of about $1\,\mathrm{m}$ has a period near $2\,\mathrm{s}$, each swing taking roughly one second.
cards.searchQuery: simple pendulum period 1 meter numeric

cards.title: What is the moment of inertia of a uniform solid sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$ about an axis through its center?
cards.body:
$I = \tfrac{2}{5}MR^2$

A thin spherical shell has $I = \tfrac{2}{3}MR^2$; the solid sphere's is smaller because more of its mass lies near the axis.

Tip: remember the order $\tfrac{2}{5} < \tfrac{1}{2} < 1$ (solid sphere, disk, hoop) for the rolling race.
cards.searchQuery: moment of inertia solid sphere two fifths M R squared
